title: The Apology You Keep Waiting For May Never Come. What Will You Do With Your Heart Until Then?
paragraphs: The Apology You Keep Waiting For May Never Come. What Will You Do With Your Heart Until Then?

When the person who wounded you refuses to admit what they did, Jesus does not ask you to call evil good. He calls you to place justice in hands strong enough to carry it—so the person who hurt you does not keep owning your heart.
Maybe you have already imagined the conversation.
More times than you would admit.
They finally sit across from you.
Their defenses are gone.
Their voice is different now.
And at last, they say the words you have needed to hear:
“I was wrong.”
“I hurt you.”
“You didn’t deserve what I did.”
“I lied.”
“I betrayed you.”
“I should have protected you.”
“I should have believed you.”
“I should never have treated you that way.”
“Please forgive me.”
And somewhere inside that imagined moment, something in your chest finally loosens.
Because perhaps you have spent months—or years—believing that healing begins when they finally understand what they did to you.
But what happens if they never do?
What happens if the apology never comes?
What happens if the person who broke something inside you sleeps peacefully while you are still trying to understand how to live with the pieces?
What happens if they rewrite the story?
What happens if they minimize it?
What happens if they blame you?
What happens if they move forward with their life while you are still carrying consequences they helped create?
And what happens if they die without ever saying they were sorry?
That question can feel almost unbearable.
Because unresolved injustice creates a peculiar kind of prison.
The door may be open, but your heart keeps waiting for someone else to walk into the room and unlock it.
This is where the Gospel speaks with startling tenderness—and startling strength.
Romans 12:19 says:
“Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, ‘Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.’”
The Greek begins with one word that matters more than we sometimes realize:
Ἀγαπητοί — agapētoi.
“Beloved.”
Before Paul speaks about vengeance, he speaks about identity.
Beloved.
Not forgotten.
Not invisible.
Not disposable.
Beloved.
God does not begin His instruction to wounded Christians by scolding them for being hurt.
He addresses them as people who are loved.
Then comes the difficult command:
μὴ ἑαυτοὺς ἐκδικοῦντες — mē heautous ekdikountes
Do not avenge yourselves.
And then:
δότε τόπον τῇ ὀργῇ — dote topon tē orgē
Literally, “give place to wrath.”
In context, Paul is telling believers to step away from personal vengeance and leave judgment to God.
Then he reaches back into the Hebrew Scriptures, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35:
לִי נָקָם וְשִׁלֵּם — li naqam veshillem
“Vengeance is Mine, and recompense.”
This does not mean God is asking you to pretend nothing happened.
It means something almost frighteningly freeing:
You are not the final court.
You do not have to become the executioner of the person who wounded you in order for their wrong to matter.
God saw it.
God knows it.
And God does not need the offender's cooperation before He can begin healing you.
Read that again.
God does not need their apology before He can begin restoring your heart.
Somebody reading this has spent years emotionally standing beside a mailbox waiting for a letter that may never arrive.
Maybe it was your father.
Your mother.
Your husband.
Your wife.
Your ex.
A sibling.
A pastor.
A church leader.
A friend you trusted with things you had never told anyone.
Maybe someone publicly humiliated you and privately acted as though nothing happened.
Maybe somebody betrayed your confidence.
Maybe someone abandoned you when you needed them most.
Maybe they cheated.
Maybe they lied about you.
Maybe they manipulated you and then convinced everyone else that you were the problem.
Maybe you confronted them—and instead of repentance, you received excuses.
Maybe the wound became even deeper because they refused to acknowledge that there was a wound at all.
There are injuries caused by what people do.
And then there are injuries caused by their refusal to admit they did it.
Sometimes the second wound hurts almost as much as the first.
Because an apology says:
I see what happened.
I acknowledge your pain.
I accept responsibility.
And when those words never come, part of us begins screaming:
“Does anybody see this?”
Jesus does.
That changes everything.
But it does not make everything easy.
Christian forgiveness is often spoken about so carelessly that wounded people begin believing Scripture requires them to become emotionally dishonest.
It does not.
Forgiveness does not require calling evil good.
Forgiveness does not require pretending betrayal did not matter.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Forgiveness does not mean every broken relationship must return to exactly what it was before.
Forgiveness does not require placing yourself back into an unsafe situation merely to prove that you are spiritual.
Scripture itself distinguishes forgiveness from reconciliation.
Romans 12:18 says:
“If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all.”
Those words matter:
If possible.
So far as it depends on you.
Reconciliation involves more than one heart.
Trust involves demonstrated faithfulness.
Repentance bears fruit.
Consequences may remain.
Boundaries may remain.
Wisdom may require distance.
You can forgive someone and still recognize that giving them the same access to your life would be foolish.
You can release vengeance without restoring privileges.
You can pray for somebody without pretending they are trustworthy.
You can refuse hatred while refusing manipulation.
You can desire their salvation while recognizing that reconciliation may require repentance and change.
And yes—you can forgive while tears are still running down your face.
Forgiveness is not amnesia.
It is surrendering the throne.
It is saying:
“God, I will not spend the rest of my life trying to become You.”
Because that is what vengeance quietly asks of us.
It asks us to become judge, jury, historian, prosecutor, and executioner.
It asks us to keep reopening the courtroom every night.
It asks us to rehearse the evidence.
Exhibit A.
Exhibit B.
Exhibit C.
Remember what they said?
Remember what they did?
Remember how nobody defended you?
Remember how they got away with it?
Again.
Again.
Again.
And every rehearsal feels as though we are preserving justice.
But sometimes we are only preserving the wound.
There is a difference between remembering what happened wisely and continually drinking from what happened bitterly.
You may have every reason to be angry.
The question is what your anger is becoming.
Paul does not tell believers that evil is imaginary.
Just two verses later, Romans 12:21 says:
“Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”
Notice the assumption.
Evil exists.
Something really happened.
Something really was wrong.
But now there is another danger.
The evil that happened to you can begin producing evil inside you.
The betrayal can become bitterness.
The injustice can become obsession.
The rejection can become an identity.
The wound can become a permanent address.
And suddenly, someone who may no longer even be present in your life is still determining what kind of person you are becoming.
That is too much power to give them.
Maybe this is where Jesus is meeting you.
Not asking you to deny what happened.
Not asking you to manufacture warm feelings toward someone who devastated you.
Not asking you to pretend justice does not matter.
He is asking you to hand Him the case.
All of it.
The evidence.
The unanswered questions.
The conversations you never got to have.
The confession they never made.
The reputation they damaged.
The years you cannot recover.
The money you lost.
The childhood you should have had.
The marriage you thought would survive.
The friendship you believed would last.
The church experience that left you afraid to trust Christians again.
The words you still hear when the room becomes quiet.
Give Him the case.
Because the hands that were pierced for you are strong enough to hold what happened to you.
And this is where Christianity becomes radically different from shallow positivity.
The Gospel never says injustice does not matter.
Look at the cross.
The cross tells us sin matters so profoundly that reconciliation with God required something far greater than pretending it never happened.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, bore sin at Calvary.
Justice was not dismissed.
Grace was purchased at immeasurable cost.
Romans 5:8 tells us:
“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
And now comes the uncomfortable part.
The Gospel does not permit us to divide humanity neatly into innocent people like us and sinners like them.
They sinned against you.
Perhaps terribly.
But you also need grace.
So do I.
We may not have committed their particular sin, and saying that does not minimize what they did.
But before the holiness of God, every one of us stands in desperate need of mercy.
That is why the Christian does not surrender vengeance because evil does not deserve judgment.
We surrender vengeance because judgment belongs ultimately to God.
And because at the cross, we discovered that the Judge we entrust ourselves to is also the Savior who offered mercy to us.
This is scandalous grace.
Jesus does not merely rescue respectable people.
He saves sinners.
Liars can repent.
Adulterers can repent.
Abusers can repent.
The proud can repent.
The bitter can repent.
The people who wounded us can repent.
And wounded people who have begun living from hatred can repent too.
Nobody is beyond the reach of Christ while there is still breath and opportunity to turn to Him.
But grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings sinners out of darkness.
That distinction matters.
The Jesus who said, “Father, forgive them,” while being crucified is the same Jesus Scripture presents as the righteous Judge.
Mercy and justice do not become enemies in Him.
So perhaps the prayer tonight is not:
“Jesus, make me forget.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, make me free.”
Free from needing their remorse before you can breathe again.
Free from checking whether life has punished them yet.
Free from imaginary arguments in the shower.
Free from stalking their happiness and secretly resenting every photograph where they appear to be doing fine.
Free from hoping their life collapses just so your pain will finally feel validated.
Free from needing everyone to understand your side before you can have peace.
Free from allowing the worst thing somebody did to you to become the central story of who you are.
Because you are more than what happened to you.
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not “betrayed.”
Not “abandoned.”
Not “divorced.”
Not “rejected.”
Not “humiliated.”
Not “forgotten.”
Not “the one they hurt.”
In Christ, you are His.
And perhaps that is why Romans begins this painful instruction with:
Ἀγαπητοί.
Beloved.
Before God asks you to release vengeance, He reminds you that you are loved.
Because releasing vengeance without knowing you are loved feels like losing.
But releasing vengeance into the hands of a Father who sees everything is different.
It becomes trust.
Maybe they never say sorry.
God is still God.
Maybe they never admit the truth.
God still knows it.
Maybe people believe their version.
God is not confused.
Maybe earthly justice comes.
Maybe it does not come in the form or timing you hoped for.
God remains righteous.

And none of this means you should remain silent about ongoing harm. Depending on what happened, wisdom may include confronting wrongdoing, seeking pastoral or professional counsel, reporting crimes or abuse to appropriate authorities, establishing boundaries, pursuing lawful justice, or getting somewhere safe.
Romans 12:19 is not a command to protect wrongdoing from consequences.
It is a command not to seize God's place through personal vengeance.
There is a profound difference between seeking legitimate justice and being consumed by revenge.
One says, “This wrong must be addressed appropriately.”
The other says, “I cannot rest until I personally make you hurt.”
Jesus wants more for your heart than that prison.
And perhaps the most difficult realization is this:
The apology you keep waiting for may never come.
But Jesus already came.
The person who wounded you may never kneel before you in repentance.
But Christ already carried a cross for sinners.
They may never give you the words you thought you needed in order to move forward.
But Christ can meet you in the place those words never reached.
He can heal without rewriting history.
He can restore without pretending.
He can soften your heart without making you naive.
He can teach you forgiveness without destroying your boundaries.
He can remove hatred without requiring foolish trust.
He can give you peace while the unanswered questions remain unanswered.
That is the miracle.
Not that the past suddenly becomes acceptable.
But that the past stops being your master.
There comes a moment when you realize healing is not getting the person who wounded you to finally become the person you needed them to be.
Healing is discovering that Jesus is sufficient even where they failed you.
Maybe your hands have been clenched around this story for years.
Maybe nobody knows how angry you still are.
Maybe you smile when their name is mentioned, but something inside you turns cold.
Maybe you have prayed about it before and then picked the case right back up.
Bring it again.
Jesus is not intimidated by how many times you have struggled to release it.
Tell Him the truth.
“Lord, what they did was wrong.”
“Lord, I still want them to admit it.”
“Lord, part of me still wants them to hurt.”
“Lord, I do not know how to forgive this.”
“Lord, I am tired.”
“Lord, judge rightly.”
“Lord, protect me from becoming what pain is trying to turn me into.”
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.”
That is not weakness.
That is surrender.
And surrender is sometimes where healing finally stops waiting for permission from the person who caused the wound.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
You do not have to pretend to be farther along than you are.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
But if this truth can reach one wounded person through you, sharing becomes a simple act of service.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God's blessing, prove your devotion, or make you more righteous. Jesus alone saves, and His grace cannot be bought.
But one genuine way believers can glorify God is by willingly supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it.
But before you leave this page, there is one more question.
Not for the person who hurt you.
For you.
If the apology never comes...
will you allow their silence to decide how the rest of your heart lives?
Or will you place the case into the scarred hands of Jesus and finally let the Judge be Judge, the Savior be Savior, and your wounded heart begin learning how to live again?
The scandal may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Because Jesus still redeems what people thought they permanently ruined.
You may never hear them say, “I’m sorry”—but you can still live long enough to hear your own heart say, “Jesus, I’m finally letting You carry this.”
